# Language models
## Review
- Language models predict the likelihood of a sequence of words
  - Applications include auto-completion, speech recognition, and more
- In the bigram model, the probability of $w_k$ only depends on the previous word, $w_{k-1}$

$$P(w_{1:n}) \approx \prod_{k=1}^n P(w_k|w_{k-1})$$

- $n$-gram language models generalize this to longer sequences of words

# Language models
## Limitations of n-gram language models
1. Insufficient data to sufficiently model language generation
2. Complex models become intractable to compute
3. Limited information on word order

# Language models
## Advances in neural language models
- Over the past decade language models have developed due to three factors:

    1. Availability of large text corpora
    2. Advances in computer processing, notably Graphics Processing Units (GPUs)
    3. Innovations in neural network architecture

# Language models
## From static to contextualized embeddings
- Word2vec learns a single vector for each word, averaging across its different uses
  - e.g. "crane" as a bird, construction equipment, or movement
- Contextualized embeddings allow the vector for a word to vary according to its context
- The *attention* mechanism makes this possible

# Large language models
## Foundation models and transfer learning
- Large language models (LLMs) are described as \textbf{foundation models} insofar as pre-trained models serve as a foundation for other tasks (Bommasani et al. 2021)
- \textbf{Transfer learning} describes the process through which a model is adapted to new tasks

\tiny Bommasani, Rishi, et al. 2021. "On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models." *arXiv*:2108.07258.

\tiny \centering Decoders take tokens as input and generate tokens. Encoders produce a vector representation of each input token. Encoder-decoders take tokens as input and generate a series of tokens. Jurafsky and Martin 2026

## Predicting the next word
LLMs predict the next *token*, usually a word or part of a word.

# Generating text
## Autoregressive generation
```{r, out.height="62%", fig.align="center"}
include_graphics('../../../img/slp3_generation.png')
```
\tiny \centering The model generates text by sampling a word from the distribution, adding it to the context, and repeating the process. Jurafsky and Martin 2026

# Generating text
## Sampling and temperature
- The *temperature* controls how random the sampling is
    - Near 0, the model always picks the most likely word, making it more deterministic
    - Higher temperatures make it more likely that less probable words are used

## Training compute over time
Most companies no longer disclose the size of their models, so the compute used for training is a common measure of scale.
```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=3, out.height="54%", fig.align="center"}
library(tidyverse)
epoch <- read_csv("../data/epoch_language_models.csv")
labels <- c("Transformer" = "Transformer", "BERT-Large" = "BERT",
            "GPT-3 175B (davinci)" = "GPT-3", "GPT-4 (Mar 2023)" = "GPT-4",
            "Llama 3.1-405B" = "Llama 3.1", "DeepSeek-R1" = "DeepSeek-R1",
            "gpt-oss-120b" = "gpt-oss", "Grok 4" = "Grok 4")
epoch |>
  mutate(open_weights = if_else(open_weights == "Yes", "Open weights", "Closed"),
         label = labels[model]) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = compute, color = open_weights)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(aes(label = label), size = 3, na.rm = TRUE,
                            show.legend = FALSE, min.segment.length = 0,
                            nudge_y = 1.5, label.size = 0.1, seed = 1) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Training compute (FLOP)", color = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.85, 0.15))
```

# Prompting
## Text-to-text models
- Early models like BERT work more like standard machine learning techniques
    - e.g. extract an embedding for a term, fine-tune to predict a label given the input
- Text-to-text models take text as input and produce text as output\*
- This natural language interface makes it easy to transfer to new tasks and enables chat interfaces

\tiny \* Raffel, Colin, Noam Shazeer, Adam Roberts, Katherine Lee, Sharan Narang, Michael Matena, Yanqi Zhou, Wei Li, and Peter J. Liu. 2020. "Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer." *Journal of Machine Learning Research* 21(140): 1–67.

# Prompting
## Context windows
- The *context window* defines the amount of text a model can process at once, measured in tokens
- Context windows have been increasing over time:
    - BERT (2018): 512
    - GPT-3 (2020): 2,048
    - GPT-4 Turbo (2023): 128,000
    - Claude 3 (2024): 200,000
    - Gemini 1.5 Pro (2024): 1,000,000

# Prompting
## User and system prompts
- *Prompts* guide the model to generate specific outputs
    - \textbf{User prompts} result in a single output
        - e.g. "Is the following text positive or negative?"
    - \textbf{System prompts} guide overall model behavior
        - e.g. "You are a helpful assistant ... "

# Prompting
## Prompt engineering
- An emerging field known as *prompt engineering* considers how to effectively design prompts
    - Art or science?
- Some systems can automatically refine and enhance prompts
    - e.g. ChatGPT rewrote user prompts to DALL-E 3 to make better images, and to diversify demographic representation in outputs

# Post-training
## Reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF)
- LLMs are pre-trained as language models but can be adapted to more general tasks by further training
- RLHF involves using feedback to guide a model's behavior and is critical to contemporary chatbots
    - Feedback used to make models "more helpful" and "less harmful"

\tiny Ouyang, Long, et al. 2022. "Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback." In *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems* 35, 27730–44.

# Post-training
## RLHF phases
```{r, out.width="84%", fig.align="center"}
include_graphics('../../../img/rlhf_instructgpt.png')
```
\tiny \centering Ouyang et al. 2022

# Post-training
## Direct preference optimization (DPO)
- RLHF trains a separate *reward model* on human preferences, then uses reinforcement learning to optimize the LLM against it
- DPO skips the reward model and trains the LLM directly on pairs of preferred and rejected responses
    - Simpler, more stable, and cheaper than RLHF

\tiny Rafailov, Rafael, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Christopher D. Manning, Stefano Ermon, and Chelsea Finn. 2023. "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model Is Secretly a Reward Model." In *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems* 36, 53728–41.

# Reasoning models
## Learning to reason
- Recent models are further trained using reinforcement learning to generate intermediate reasoning steps before answering
    - e.g. OpenAI's o1, DeepSeek-R1
- Rewards come from tasks with verifiable answers, such as math problems and coding tests

\tiny Guo, Daya, et al. 2025. "DeepSeek-R1 Incentivizes Reasoning in LLMs Through Reinforcement Learning." *Nature* 645(8081): 633–38.

# Agents
## What are agents?
- LLMs are increasingly used as *agents* that can use tools and pursue a goal over many steps
    - The model chooses an action, such as searching the web or running code, observes the result, and decides what to do next
- Coding agents like Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex can write, run, and debug code across a project

# Text classification with LLMs
## Interaction modalities
- Three core ways to use LLMs:

    1. Chat in browser (e.g. ChatGPT)
    2. Code via API (e.g. OpenAI API)
    3. Code via local model (e.g. Llama on a laptop)

- Chat interfaces are good for experimentation, but code-based interaction is necessary for systematic research

# Text classification with LLMs
## Zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuning
- Pre-trained LLMs can be used in several ways that differ from conventional supervised machine learning:
    - *Zero-shot learning*: LLM makes a prediction based on a prompt alone
    - *Few-shot learning*: LLM makes a prediction based on a prompt and one or more training examples
    - *Fine-tuning*: Training data are fed into the LLM and its weights are updated to adapt to the task

# Exercise
## Prompt engineering for text classification
- Task: Predict the sentiment of 100 reviews from last week's test set using a small LLM on your laptop
    - Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (0.5B parameters), run using `localLLM`
- Edit the prompt to improve the scores and reduce the number of responses without a sentiment
    - Zero-shot: Instructions only
    - Few-shot: Instructions plus one or more labeled examples

# Exercise
## Installing `localLLM`
`localLLM` runs models locally using `llama.cpp`.
```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, tidy=FALSE, mysize=TRUE, size='\\footnotesize'}
install.packages("localLLM",
                 repos = c("https://eddieyang211.r-universe.dev",
                           "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
# Restart R (Session > Restart R), then run the rest
library(localLLM)
install_localLLM() # Downloads the backend
```

# Exercise
## Generating text
The model (491 MB) is downloaded the first time it is used.
```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, tidy=FALSE, mysize=TRUE, size='\\footnotesize'}
model <- paste0("https://huggingface.co/Qwen/",
                "Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-GGUF/resolve/main/",
                "qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf")

quick_llama("What is sentiment analysis?", model_path = model,
            verbosity = -1) |>
  cat()
```

# Exercise
## Loading the test set
Reviews are truncated to 500 characters to keep the inputs short. The split is the same as last week, and we take a random sample of 100 test reviews.
```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, tidy=FALSE, mysize=TRUE, size='\\footnotesize'}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
d <- read_tsv("../data/imdb_reviews_sample.tsv") |>
  mutate(text = str_trunc(text, 500))

set.seed(76543)
review_split <- initial_split(d, strata = "sentiment",
                              prop = 0.8)
test <- testing(review_split) |> slice_sample(n = 100)
```

# Exercise
## Writing a prompt
`classify` adds a review to the prompt and returns the response, stopping after 10 tokens.
```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, tidy=FALSE, mysize=TRUE, size='\\footnotesize'}
prompt <- ""

classify <- function(text) {
  quick_llama(paste0(prompt, "\n\nReview: ", text),
              model_path = model, max_tokens = 10,
              clean = TRUE, hash = FALSE, verbosity = -1)
}
```

# Exercise
## Classifying a single review
Change `i` to try other reviews.
```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, tidy=FALSE, mysize=TRUE, size='\\footnotesize'}
i <- 1
classify(test$text[i])
test$sentiment[i]
```

# Exercise
## Classifying all 100 reviews
Why is the `str_detect()` function necessary?
```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, tidy=FALSE, mysize=TRUE, size='\\footnotesize'}
results <- test |>
  mutate(
    response = map_chr(text, classify, .progress = TRUE),
    prediction = case_when(
      str_detect(response, "[Pp]ositive") ~ "pos",
      str_detect(response, "[Nn]egative") ~ "neg"),
    prediction = factor(prediction, levels = c("neg", "pos")),
    sentiment = factor(sentiment, levels = c("neg", "pos")))
```

# Exercise
## Evaluating performance
Responses without a valid label are `NA` and excluded from the scores.
```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, tidy=FALSE, mysize=TRUE, size='\\footnotesize'}
results |> count(sentiment, prediction)
sum(is.na(results$prediction)) # Responses without a sentiment

review_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, precision, recall, f_meas)
results |>
  review_metrics(truth = sentiment, estimate = prediction)
```
\tiny As last week, precision and recall refer to negative reviews.

## Structured output
- Many APIs support *structured output*, which restricts responses to a predefined format, such as a set of labels
- This ensures that only valid labels are produced

## Choosing an approach

# Interpretability
## Opening the black box
- Conventional machine learning models offer limited interpretability, even less so for complex neural networks, and worse as size increases
- An area of research known as *mechanistic interpretability* reverse-engineers model behavior by analyzing internal feature activations

# Interpretability
## Features
- Researchers have identified millions of interpretable features in LLMs that represent different concepts

\tiny Templeton, Adly, et al. 2024. "Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet." *Transformer Circuits Thread*. \url{https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/scaling-monosemanticity/}

\tiny \centering The feature activates on text and images related to the bridge in many languages. \url{https://www.anthropic.com/research/mapping-mind-language-model}

# Interpretability
## Circuits
- *Circuit tracing* maps the steps a model takes to produce an output, e.g. planning a rhyme before writing a line of poetry
- But these methods only explain part of a model's computation, and only for some prompts

\tiny Lindsey, Jack, et al. 2025. "On the Biology of a Large Language Model." *Transformer Circuits Thread*. \url{https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html}

# Interpretability
## Circuits: multi-step reasoning
```{r, out.height="64%", fig.align="center"}
include_graphics('../../../img/circuit_dallas_austin.png')
```
\tiny \centering To name the capital of the state containing Dallas, the model represents Texas as an intermediate step. Lindsey et al. 2025. \url{https://www.anthropic.com/research/tracing-thoughts-language-model}

# Interpretability
## Are reasoning traces faithful?
- Reasoning models output intermediate steps before answering, but these traces are not necessarily a faithful account of how the model reached its answer
- When a prompt contains a cue that biases the answer, such as a hint, models often follow it without mentioning it in their reasoning

\tiny Turpin, Miles, Julian Michael, Ethan Perez, and Samuel R. Bowman. 2023. "Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting." In *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems* 36, 74952–65.

Chen, Yanda, et al. 2025. "Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think." *arXiv*:2505.05410.

# Reliability
## Hallucinations
- LLMs are trained to predict text sequences without adherence to formal logic or truth—raising reliability issues
    - Outputs can range from meaningful and accurate to incorrect or misleading ("hallucinations" or "confabulations")

# Reliability
## Why do LLMs hallucinate?
- Next-word pre-training produces errors on facts that appear only once in the training data, such as a person's birthday
- Evaluations that only score accuracy reward guessing over admitting uncertainty
    - Answering "I don't know" always scores zero, while a guess might be right

\tiny Kalai, Adam Tauman, Ofir Nachum, Santosh S. Vempala, and Edwin Zhang. 2026. "Evaluating Large Language Models for Accuracy Incentivizes Hallucinations." *Nature* 653(8116): 1047–51.

# Bias and ethics
## Stereotypes and biases
- Models learn stereotypes from data and make biased outputs
- LLMs amplify this risk due to pre-training on vast amounts of unvetted data
- Alignment and reinforcement learning are used to adapt commercial models, but biases remain

# Bias and ethics
## Ethical questions
- Analyzing sensitive data poses risks, potentially violating privacy regulations (e.g. inputs to ChatGPT may violate IRB guidelines on data sharing)
- Ethical dilemmas also arise from LLM use in research settings
- The rapid development of technology outpaces consensus on ethical guidelines, necessitating cautious and informed application in research

# Transparency and reproducibility
## Transparency
- Advanced generative AI models, often developed by corporations, lack transparency regarding their training data
- This opacity complicates assessing the influence of pre-training on model outputs

# Transparency and reproducibility
## Reproducibility
- Reproducibility is undermined by the stochasticity of LLMs
    - Identical prompts can lead to varied outputs
- Model updates and retirements by corporations can further impede the ability to reproduce results

# Closed versus open models
- The most powerful models are controlled by a handful of corporations
    - GPT (OpenAI), Gemini (Google), Claude (Anthropic)
    - These models are easy to use via APIs with minimal programming experience
- Open-weight alternatives include Llama (Meta), Gemma (Google), Qwen (Alibaba), and DeepSeek
    - Smaller models can run on a laptop
    - Larger models require access to high-performance compute environments and more technical knowledge

# Closed versus open models
## Improving open-weight models
- The best open-weight models now trail the best closed models by about four months

\tiny Edwards, Jack, and Luke Emberson. 2026. "Open Models Lag State-of-the-Art Closed Models by 4 Months." *Epoch AI*. \url{https://epoch.ai/data-insights/open-closed-eci-gap}

# Closed versus open models
## Open weights versus open source
- *Open weights* does not mean *open source*
    - Training data and code generally not released
    - Fully open models like Olmo 3 (Ai2) also release training data, code, and checkpoints

\tiny Team Olmo, et al. 2025. "Olmo 3." *arXiv*:2512.13961.

# Closed versus open models
- Advantages of open-source models:
    - Public weights and training data
    - More controlled and reproducible
    - Lower privacy risks
    - More customizable

\tiny Spirling, Arthur. 2023. "Why Open-Source Generative AI Models Are an Ethical Way Forward for Science." *Nature* 616(7957): 413.
    
# Recommendations
## Reporting LLM-based research
- Checklist for reporting studies that use LLMs in the behavioral and social sciences
    - Scope of LLM use and the degree of human oversight
    - Model details: exact model and version, access mode, date, and settings such as temperature
    - Exact prompts, including system prompts and examples

\tiny Feuerriegel, Stefan, et al. 2026. "A Reporting Checklist for Large Language Models in Behavioural Science." *Nature Human Behaviour* 10(7): 1182–86. Checklist: \url{https://www.llm-checklist.com}


# Summary
- Transformers use attention to represent words in context
- LLMs are pre-trained on vast corpora and adapted to new tasks through fine-tuning or prompting
- Post-training, reasoning, and tool use extend LLMs beyond next-word prediction
- Zero- and few-shot learning reduce the need for training data, but predictions still need to be validated
- Whether LLMs understand language, access meaning, think, and reason is debated
- LLMs pose challenges for reliability, bias, ethics, transparency, and reproducibility
